utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please call the case, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. So this Thursday I greet the accused, the counsel, and all the representatives of the Prosecution offices and all the persons who assist us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: It would be very useful if we could break around 4.00. We would have 20 minutes' break, and we would resume at 20 minutes past 6.00 [as interpreted], and we could finish at 6.00 if possible. The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Bagaric?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Sir, the document that we were looking at yesterday, which was P04527, and we were looking together, you and I, at the names of the people who had the authority to grant free passage and freedom of movement for, amongst other things, humanitarian organisations. We saw you at number 9. We saw the names of some of the accused. At number 3, Ivo Lucic, a gentleman who was also at the Tomislavgrad meeting that we looked at the very beginning of my questioning of you yesterday in December 1991. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Yes. Ivo Lucic, the gentleman there at number 3, he was also at that meeting that we spent some time looking at, the meeting in Tomislavgrad.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the meeting. I was at the meeting, but I'm not sure that Ivo Lucic was there also. I don't remember Ivo Lucic being there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to take our time to check it now. We have the document, and the transcript will show. At number 8, Veso Vegar, was the head of the administration for information and propaganda; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether that is right or not. I believe that he was in charge of the department that I was in charge of addressing the media or talking to the media, something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to ask you about him, because do you recall when we looked at a document that Ms. Nozica showed to you, the document in which the ABiH write to you asking for aid? It's our document 2D00122. It's in -- I'm so sorry. It's in -- perhaps if we could just bring it up on the screen. 2D0122. This is the letter from Arif Pasalic that we looked at that's dated the 9th of June and which appears to have led to you sending a quantity of medicines to the east bank. Do you recall that? Can you just look with me at the first paragraph of the text of the letter where it says: "Considering that through the media you announced the medical cooperation and aid to the wounded and sick persons, we hereby address you as follows." Can you help us just a little bit with that, please, Dr. Bagaric. The letter seems to be suggesting that the HVO, perhaps the HVO medical staff to whom it's addressed, but certainly the HVO, have been announcing through the media that they'll help the other side. Was that what was going on in June of 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 9th of June, and this was on the 9th of June, I already spoke about this document, and I said that prior to that, we had offered help to the east side, and I suppose that this is the answer to our previous offer of cooperation, the cooperation that I have been talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Bagaric, yesterday, I'm not criticising you in any way at all, but you and I perhaps spent longer dealing with some topics that then was necessary, and the President of the Tribunal asked you last night if you could just try to answer the question that I'm asking you, and the question is this: Where we see Arif Pasalic writing that someone on your side has been making announcements through the media about giving aid and medical cooperation, I'm asking you if that had happened, that at about this time in 1993, on behalf of the HVO, announcements were being made in the media to that effect. I'm not asking you a question that could be answered by the answer that you gave.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. On the 9th of June, of course I can't say whether this was announced at that time. However, I assume that our openness for cooperation was made known through the media, and then the response to that was this request, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you help us as one of the people who was in Mostar dealing with these issues, was Veso Vegar himself involved in announcements of that kind?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I wouldn't know that. I assume that this was aired on one or the two radios without Veso Vegar, because both the west side and the east side had their respective radio stations, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Can I put this to you, you have a think about it and then you tell us what you think: In the summer of 1993, aid, medical aid, humanitarian aid, had become a political issue. What do you think about that, Dr. Bagaric?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I spoke about that, and I said that to a certain extent the east side, i.e., the Muslim leadership, in a certain way did not match our request -- our offers for assistance, and I thought this was a political issue. I thought that such orders for non-implementations arrived from the top of the political leadership. That's what I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you. And it had become a political issue for the HVO as well, hadn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I'm convinced, rather, that this was never an issue that the HVO had a position similar to the position of the other side in this particular case. So I wouldn't say that the answer is positive, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: The international community were making representations in a number of different places, but those representations were to the effect that East Mostar should be assisted, and you, the HVO, and those with control of the aid to Mostar, you knew about that, didn't you? And you were under pressure, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally was under no pressure, and I can only speak on my own behalf. Whoever addressed me from the international community in terms of the transport of the wounded or some other activities, I helped as much as I could. Your Honours, when I addressed the generals who are present here today and when I conveyed the message of the others who needed my help, then I was given their support, and I was able to provide that help. I don't know of any other requests of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to suggest to you that there was pressure, both locally and at international level, and I'm going to ask you to look with me, please, at this document, P05080.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] I will find it. It's okay. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: It's another presidential transcript, and this transcript tell us that Mate Boban is at the presidential palace of Franjo Tudjman on the 15th of September, 1993, and the delegation of the Croatia Republic of Herceg-Bosna is welcomed by him, and he goes on to say, does President Tudjman, that Croatia was under pressure, official pressure, from the EU as a whole and from individual states. And we're going to see the topics in just a moment: "Over the past 14 days, I received at least five or six Official Notes from the European Union, the United States of America, France, and Germany. They all requested that we make as many concessions to the Muslims as possible, and they all threatened us with sanctions because of the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina. "They even went as far as sending us a warning that they would cancel our special-guest status at the European Council Assembly." And then these words: "In such, they clearly put your camps and humanitarian convoys and so on in the first place." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And that is a record of Mr. Tudjman telling the Herceg-Bosna delegation that he's under a great deal of pressure because a lot of different countries in the EU are very concerned, particularly about the camps, and we dealt with them yesterday, and about humanitarian convoys. And I want to ask you this: Isn't the position that pressure of that kind, as relayed by Tudjman to Boban, made its way down to the ground in Mostar and that from time to time of course some aid was allowed through? That's the true position, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise to you and to my learned friend Laws. It seems to me that it's necessary to point out something that my learned friend Karnavas pointed out as happening; that is, laying the factual basis for a question, and in that way to 2D122, which is Bruno Stojic Defence document is tied with events which took place in the summer of 1993 and then the next question refers to the month of September 1993. The Trial Chamber knows only too well that on the 30th of June, 1993, was the break point in the relationship between the HVO and the BH Army. And any question that ignores that fact or makes an attempt to portray something that was happening in the summer of 1993 as something that was happening in June of that year simply is not correct. I believe that this should be recorded, and I would kindly ask the Trial Chamber to intervene in that sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Alaburic. You needn't say so. The Judges are perfectly informed of this. If you want to say it in a very open way, you could come back on this question. Here we've lost three minutes for nothing. Would please continue, Mr. Laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Before I do, may I respectfully say that that, of course, is an argument that could be advanced, but it doesn't go anyway to suggesting that the question is improper. I'm talking about pressure being applied, and the witness understands that, and the Trial Chamber has a full grasp of history, and in the interests perhaps of moving along, I just wanted to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Bagaric, in East Mostar you --

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I don't know what is it that I understand or appreciate. You're saying that I understand something, but what is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I was answering an interruption made by one of the counsel, not by you, and I'm going to continue now by asking you questions if I may, Dr. Bagaric. Dr. Bagaric, the position in East Mostar was - I don't think you disagree with this - a very, very poor one so far as the plight of the civilians was concerned. We're not disagreeing about that, are we?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection. In a question worded in this way, we have to contain a reference of time. It has to be -- contain a when. We all know that the events were happening at a speed of lightning, that the characteristics of the conflict changed gradually from one day to another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, the document which the Prosecution is using concerning international pressure is a meeting of the 15th of September, 1993. Therefore, the answer is in the document. What's the purpose of intervening? Of course the question has to do with the 15th September 1993 and not January.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: If we can just try and move on, Dr. Bagaric. The position was that from time to time during the course of the East Mostar civilians being very largely cut off from aid, from time to time the HVO allowed material through. And before anybody interrupts, I'm talking about the position as it was from June of 1993 through to April of the following year. That's the position, isn't it, Dr. Bagaric?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time nobody fared well, in Mostar, either on the east bank or the west bank. It was less good on the east bank than on the west. And the same applied to the entire Central Bosnia, especially when it came to Croats. This was a period when the situation was not good due to war operations, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: The position was that from time to time you sent them medicines and some other material, but it was not enough, not enough, to go anywhere near to changing the situation in East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to object to that, and I'm going to start objecting because the assumption is that there was enough to go around. He needs to lay a foundation. Where is it that he could show -- because he's -- he's now putting his case that there is enough. Where is the foundation that there was all this overwhelming aid that was available for both sides?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, we looked at two documents yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here also you're intervening at the wrong moment. The Prosecutor has his own thesis concerning the medicines. There weren't enough because they were blocked by the HVO. This is the Prosecution's position. Let the witness answer. Let him answer. What he will say will have much more weight than whatever you may say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He can put that question as long as there's a foundation. When there is no foundation, it's pure speculative.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: It's nothing of the kind. I laid the foundation yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the basis is the indictment. Everything is in the indictment and the preliminary motion. He's not inventing the question. He's just asking questions on what he has in his mind, the indictment and its development in the preliminary motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: We're wasting a great deal of time. Mr. Karnavas has said that there is no foundation. Yesterday I looked at two documents, 2D00714 and 2D00738, in which this witness describes the position so far as medical supplies to the West Mostar hospital as being satisfactory, and that's the position. It's not wrong. We looked at it, and I'm not going to take up any more time. So we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: -- at some stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at then, please, some of the things that you did and some of the things that were suggested, and let's look at P02782.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you did not answer the question of the -- of Mr. Laws because Mr. Karnavas interrupted. The Prosecutor has a idea about the medicines. What do you answer: Do you agree with what the Prosecutor says or do you disagree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, international organisations, including the Red Cross and the UN regularly went to the east side of Mostar, or at least very often, and from the east side we no longer had requests for medicines. I assumed at the time that they did not have any particular need for any specific medicines. That is my opinion, because as of then, we never received any more requests for medical supplies or medicines, and I state that with full responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Can we look at P02782, please, Doctor, which is under seal. And in this report we can see -- forgive me. We can see that the author is dealing with the east side at number 3. He's had contact with the east side hospital and has been provided with a list of urgent needed material and medicines: "We've arranged for the west side hospital to obtain the medicines tomorrow, tomorrow morning." You looked at that with Ms. Nozica: "HVO sanitary services have promised to take care of some part of the material, oxygen, et cetera, if the east side provides the empty bottles and pays for it (50 bottles equals 2 .000 Deutschmarks)." And then part of the offer that you were making at this time: "They have offered again to take care for all the wounded people, Muslims or Croats, including people from the east side." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Can we turn the page, please, and look at the conclusion that the EC monitors had about that. It's item 6 under "Assessment." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: "At present, the transport of wounded people from the east side to the west is totally impossible due to the snipers. If the east side hospital is not provided with the material and medicines needed, it will be closed." All right? And then we continue: "Yesterday, the ethnic cleansing on the west bank of Muslim families by HVO still went on. Strong protest against this action should be taken." So it was this gentleman's view that the offer that you were making was just one that was impossible, because people didn't want to travel from the east for fear of being shot by snipers. All right? That was his assessment. Was that the position, in fact, on the ground in East Mostar as you understood it to be in June of 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, in the month of June, on both the east and the west side of Mostar, there was a war, and nobody could guarantee anybody anything. However, I repeat that in the offers that we sent from the hospital, let me remind you we offered the Red Cross to enter our hospital, that the UNPROFOR protected the hospital and made it an ex-territorial area. If this had happened, nobody would have been wounded or killed -- and killed, and everybody who would have been transported to the hospital would have enjoyed full safety. Nobody responded to our offer, and I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Counsel, please. Microphone, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to say for the record that I did not show the witness this document, although my learned friend says I did. I just want that on the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I fully accept that, that correction, and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Let's look at the next document, which is also under seal and which deals with the topic that you've just been answering about, P02923. It's another report by the EC Monitor Mission. It's dated the 24th of June, 1993, and it has a record under item 5 of you having a discussion with the EC monitors about the proposal of exchanging doctors with the hospital of the east side. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: What was happening, according to this document, was that, first of all, it had been proposed by someone, not you, that there should be an exchange of doctors with the hospital of the east side, and you said no, that was not going to be accepted: "...will not be accepted until we achieve the freedom of movement for the HVO doctors that are obliged to work in the BiH hospitals in Travnik, Konjic, and Zenica." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that. I can see what it says there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you. And then you come up with an alternative which is this proposal that you have told us about in which a quite separate hospital should be set up which could help everybody. Yeah? Open the old hospital of Mostar, use it as a war hospital for everybody, Muslims and Croats and everybody would be treated under international supervision. That's the proposal you were making; yeah?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a very important document, so please allow me to comment on it briefly, because as I say, it's very important. In point 3 it says: "Mr. Ivan Bagaric deputy chief of the Medical Corps." So I was not the deputy, I was the chief. It doesn't mean that I wasn't at that meeting, although I, myself, don't remember this particular meeting; however we had contacts with the international community on an almost daily basis. So if these people have signed this document, then I do believe that I was there, but what is important here to mention is the following: It says that Bagaric said, under point 5, that he would not accept until freedom of movement is ensured for the HVO doctors. And I say with full responsibility here and now that it is impossible that I uttered those words. Now, what could I have said? It is this: When we offered to have our doctors from the west bank go to the east bank, nobody agreed to go, not a single person, not even the Muslims. The Muslim Bosniak physicians, they didn't agree to that either. So Ivan Bagaric, during the war, did nothing by force. I didn't force anybody to do anything. It is true that I requested, because I had a lack of cadres and physicians, and I said the Muslim Bosniaks had many more doctors in Sarajevo, Zenica, Tuzla and so on, because they were the big centres; and that our people, when I say our people, I mean our doctors, asked to leave those areas; but the Bosniak side did not allow them to do that. And so I did request of the international community to allow them to go out, to leave, because in that case we would have gained a great deal and the Muslims would not have lost much. And if you look at the text that follows, I say here you have a hospital in the middle of town, but I stayed here with full responsibility not to have that hospital opened -- it's not that this hospital was to be opened. Why? Because it was already open. It was a hospital in which we worked throughout the war right up at the front line, and that was the substance of my proposal. If we were able to work that way, then others could -- could as well. If we treated patients, others could do that the same. If we guaranteed work for our doctors, then the international community could as well following my proposal. So that's my comment on this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: The gentleman with whom you were having dealings on this topic gave evidence in this Trial Chamber. His name was Mr. Van den Grinten, a Dutch officer. Do you remember him?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember him, but if the gentleman testified, then I'm quite willing to believe that that is the document in question; so that is quite possible, but as I said, I don't remember the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: What he had to say about your proposal of the two sides having treatment in a joint hospital was that it was not realistic, not realistic. That's what he said. That is a quotation from the transcript, and it's page 21168.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I be allowed to comment just briefly?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it's very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Of course you can.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that the gentleman said so, that those were his comments, that he reported it that way, but I know that a long time ago a man once said he -- he turned, and I know that somebody killed him. I know that someone once said that you could go to the moon, and they said that he was a madman, but man did fly to the moon. So I might have been mad, too, and I was because I went ahead of my time or -- or I went in -- I was in the forefront. Now, I apologise for the vehement way in which I spoke yesterday when we were discussing politics, but when I'm speaking about this subject I know what I'm saying, and I'm saying this before this august Trial Chamber; and I'm telling you how it was, and I say that with full responsibility. It was a poor assessment by the officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, he said -- he said that it was in the wrong location and that it couldn't be -- well, you said yourself it was right on the front line. It couldn't be secured.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. Excuse me. No, no, sir. [Interpretation] Your Honours, that's the crux of the matter. Had the proposal been accepted, the Muslim Bosniak side couldn't have attacked the hospital. Do you know what the hospital looks like on the other side? If you were to look at Mr. Goldstein's report, and he was the member of the IPPNW, that is the international organisation for the struggle and prevention of nuclear war and winner of the Nobel prize, he described what the hospital looked like and published it. It was bullet riddled. It was destroyed and so on and so forth. But it carried on working. And that had that been accepted, that would not have been the case. The hostilities would have ceased, of course, over a period of time; but the situation would have changed, that's for sure. And I had support here from Mr. Bruno Stojic and the generals here, and nobody could oppose it. Had they opposed it, then I think I would have let the whole world know, published it worldwide. It would have gone to the United Nations to complain if somebody had tried to prevent it on the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I don't mean to say that intervene because I do not want to waste time, but yesterday and today, this is the first time we've heard this, you stressed the fact that according to you had the medical issue been settled, the hostilities would have ceased; and you connect all the developments to the fact that no solution was found to the medical issue. This thesis may prove true, but nobody has ever said that to us. You're the first one saying this to us. You may be right, I'm not saying you're wrong, but what you're saying is interesting. Right. I wanted this to be on record for this -- for -- so it's clear to everyone for what you're trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Would you turn the page, please, in the same document and look at the very last sentence of the final page. It's under the heading "Assessment." "We think that the HVO is not willing to deal with humanitarian aid for the east bank." All right? That's --

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What document is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: The same one we're looking at, the one in which your offer of a joint hospital was made. Exactly the same document. We haven't turned the page. I can give you the number again it's P02923. P02923.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 2923 you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: It's all right. It's never easy to find your way around. The last page of that document we were looking at a moment ago has at the end a sentence that I want to draw to your attention. Do you have that document now?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I've found it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And what it says is: "We think the HVO is not willing to deal with humanitarian aid for the east bank." Right? Can you see it says that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what it says. That's obvious in that sentence, but I don't know how he came to that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to put to you exactly how he says he came to that conclusion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hold on, Prosecutor. In the translation I can see the English word "we think." In the French version the French interpreters say we "estimon". That's a French word. There's a difference between "we think" and "nous estimon," we estimate. When we think, it is a hypothesis; and we say "nous estimon," you draw a conclusion on the basis of a situation. The English word "we think," how can it be interpreted? What was the meaning given to it by the drafter? Does he say "we think" as a hypothesis or is it we conclude as an assessment, an estimation. I want this to be on the record to avoid any mis -- or any diverging interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Can I assist in this way. The witness gave evidence its page 21055 of the transcript and this very sentence was put to him by Mr. Stringer when asking him questions. Mr. Stringer asked, it's line 6: "Read him that sentence, we think the HVO is not willing to deal humanitarian aid for the east bank. Why did you say that at that time?" He asks and the answer is: "Well for the same reasons I just explained to you. Coming with such a kind of proposal," and when we look at the transcript, he's referring back to the proposal to open the hospital, "means that you're not really willing to solve the problem on the local level."

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And I hope, Dr. Bagaric, you've been able to follow that explanation. The -- I --

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] I do apologise, but I don't understand what you said. I don't understand the explanation. It's not logical. I do apologise, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Let me try to put if in a different way. When people needed help in East Mostar, you're suggesting opening a new hospital wasn't going to help a single one of them get any kind of help of any sort. That's the position, because it was unrealistic and --

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Heaven forbid.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And you've used the comparison of somebody wanting to fly to the moon. That all depends what technology you've got available to you and what period you're living in, doesn't it? For you to say that in the summer of 1993 was unrealistic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, I'd just like to make an objection. Mr. Laws is using the term "new hospital," whereas the witness has said a number of times that it was a building which existed as a hospital, and the proposal was that that same building, that same hospital, be turned into a joint hospital. So let's be precise on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: You've got the point, Dr. Bagaric, haven't you? Your proposal wasn't one that was going to help anybody. There was no way that the two sides were going to set up a hospital of that kind, and saying it wasn't going to assist a soul, was it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with that. Absolutely not. I don't want to take up more time, so I'm not going to expound on that point any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: All right. Can I ask you, please, to turn with me to document P04346. It's another document that is under seal. It records a meeting between ECMM and a gentleman named Bozo Raguz. Did you know Bozo Raguz?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Bozo Raguz, in the political and military sense, means nothing. I don't know the man. At least at that time he wasn't somebody who was known. Bozo Raguz, no, I don't know him. I don't think the man exists, and that this name and surname has been used for someone else, that it's a mix-up of names.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: He does exist, and he is an HVO liaison officer, and in other documents that we have he's referred to a colonel, if that assists. But anyway, let's -- let's assume that there's somebody with his name. He appears to have been a mathematics teacher before the war, and he appeared anxious to help and gave a history lesson to the gentlemen whom he met in Mostar. He also had something to say on the topic of humanitarian aid, and I want to know, please, whether you heard similar things being said by members of the HVO in Mostar in the summer, autumn, winter of 1993. If you look at page 2 in the B/C/S, it's also page 2 in the English, at little (d). Do you have that paragraph, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: On humanitarian convoys he said that Mr. Prlic was now in charge of policy, and then this: " ... how can we allow humanitarian aid to pass to the aggressors"? Can you see those words?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see what it says here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: On the face of it, that is an HVO liaison officer giving expression to a point of view very different from yours. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really do apologise, Your Honours, but I really can't comment on this. I can't comment on a document I know nothing about or this man who says something here. I don't know how to answer that. Bozo Raguz, as far as I'm concerned, does not exist, and I really don't believe that there was anybody who did anything there, least of all anything important by the name of Bozo Raguz. I don't know anybody by that name. I don't think he existed. And then it would appear that he said that Prlic said something. Now, Prlic is intelligent enough not to say anything as stupid as this. I know the man, and that is what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Do you mean -- sorry, do you mean intelligent enough not to say something as stupid as this -- in what context do you mean that, please?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I want to say is this: I'm saying it in the context of the fact that a humanitarian convoy, a support to the civilian population was something that we needed, too, in Central Bosnia; and the Muslims needed it on the east bank, and that had both -- both sides worked on that subject seriously, we would have had humanitarian aid, and we wouldn't have found ourselves in the position we did. I apologise. I know we don't have time, but I have to say how we organised this route to Central Bosnia, the white road as we called it, and a humanitarian convoy to prevent the disappearance of Croats in Central Bosnia because they were no longer able to maintain their position militarily. We tried to help them and turn the eyes of the world to the suffering of the people over there and that the Muslim Bosniaks on the east bank were suffering as well, but nobody about that, and that's the difference whereas both sides suffered.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... before we lose the question completely with you telling us that both sides suffered, which, if you'll forgive me for saying so, we all know; when you said it's now 15 lines ago in the transcript that Prlic was intelligent enough not to say anything as stupid as this, what did you mean by that, please? Just ell us what you meant by saying that Mr. Prlic was intelligent enough not to say something as stupid as this?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it was stupid to prevent a convoy here. It's the humanitarian convoy as support to the civilian population. I think that was stupid.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, again we're not going to disagree about that, but the sentiments expressed by Mr. Raguz, whose identity you doubt, but the sentiments expressed by him, "how can we allow --"

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: No, you said that. "How can we allow humanitarian aid to pass to the aggressors," was that a -- was that a sentiment that you ever heard anywhere else amongst any member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Could you repeat that question, please? I really didn't understand it. Not that I didn't understand it. I wasn't concentrating hard enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Bozo Raguz - you never heard of him - he is expressing there the view that --

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Yes. We are agreed about -- he may not have heard about you, but it doesn't mean you don't exist, Doctor, does it? He expresses the view, Dr. Bagaric, that it was a mistake to allow humanitarian aid to pass to the aggressors, how could they do that; and I want to know whether the true position is that was a widespread view held by members of the HVO so far as East Mostar was concerned.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether it was the widespread view held by members of the HVO as far as East Mostar is concerned. So air asking about who it was the widespread view.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I quite understand you, but I think -- I think -- yes. I think that this observation here by somebody, by a man whom I don't know at all, cannot be held to be relevant, and it cannot reflect on the whole of the HVO. So that's my comment, and I don't wish to say any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: The Judges will have to decide whether it's relevant. The question for you is whether that's a view you heard expressed by the HVO -- by HVO members who you knew and spent each day with in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Could the witness just -- just -- I have asked several times now. If there is a genuine objection, it might have come earlier. Could the witness answer it and perhaps then counsel can say what she wishes to say, because with the greatest of respect, sometimes the witness takes his lead from what is being said by counsel and that's not, with respect, the way forward in these proceedings. I have asked it a number of times and I've been very patient. I'm just giving him this last opportunity, and I invite you, Mr. President, just to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Witness -- hold on, Ms. Nozica. Let the witness answer. The question is not complicated. You can answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that was the dominant position. There was certainly people who had their own reasons and who had suffered and had their frustrations and who displayed enormous hostility towards the opposite side and vice versa, of course, but that wasn't the dominant position, the position that prevailed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do apologise but I want to draw your attention to the fact that on page 23, line 21 and 22, this same answer was already given, that is to say the witness answered the same way he's just answered now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prosecutor, perhaps you should move on to something else, but I'd like to draw your attention, Prosecutor, to the way you interpret Mr. Raguz's words as reported in the document, in paragraph (d) of -- of two political activities. Apparently Mr. Raguz says that Mr. Prlic is in charge of policy. That's one thing. And Raguz adds, and we. It doesn't say Prlic. It says we. We can be himself. Prlic, we don't know. You agree with this. So we can encompass Prlic, Raguz, but also others, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I quite agree, and -- and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right, okay fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: -- wasn't in any way me tying Prlic to those statements. I made that very clear. The witness said that Prlic wasn't so stupid as to say something of that kind, but that's a different matter; but I completely agree with what you said, Mr. President, moving on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The witness also said that Prlic wasn't the type that would hold that point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: You're going to have to go to the transcript and work out what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The moment you start characterizing the witness's testimony, that's the moment that I begin to also characterize it because that's what the witness indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, that's not a matter that we can resolve. You'll sort it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Okay. You're all in agreement that we may encompass several persons, and we don't know exactly whom. We all agree on this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: In general, I'm in agreement with you, Mr. President; but I would like to make it clear that probably it would help if the interpreters would read actually -- or, rather, our witness would read in Croatian that particular paragraph (d), which now says: "U vezi sa humanitarnim konvojima, rekao je da je gospodin Prlic sada zaduzen," et cetera. So I would like to ask you, Dr. Bagaric, to read in Croatian paragraph (d) and then let us ask the interpreters to translate it, of course, in accordance with the original Croatian text. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] (d): "As regards humanitarian convoys, he said that Mr. Prlic was now in charge of the position as regards 'how can we allow the passage of humanitarian convoys for the aggressors'."

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise, but the original is English, not the Croatian, and we have to make a distinction here. In the English there is this word "we," whereas in the Croatian, that word does not exist. The English version has to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the one that is considered the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Laws, shall we proceed with something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: We can leave this topic in just one moment, Dr. Bagaric. The position in East Mostar we're agreed is a poor one, a very poor one that produced suffering. We don't disagree about that, you and I.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in East Mostar. I was never there. But I know that it was difficult. It was not good. Nobody had a good time there. It was the same all over Mostar, but it was particularly bad in East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: The conditions there were brought about, I'm going to put to you, as a result of actions by the HVO. Expelling Muslims from the west bank. You agree that happened, don't you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, these are two things that you are asserting. You said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... just one. Expelling Muslims from the west bank happened, didn't it, into East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happen because of the war, because of the hell. And this also happened in East Mostar and happened to Croats there. Whatever happened on one side was reciprocated on the other side, and that was the case everywhere in Mostar. I repeat, the situation was bad all over Mostar, and that's why the war had to be stopped, be put an end to.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am really embarrassed to have to do what I'm going to do for the first time in the courtroom. I'm looking at my learned friend Mr. Scott. I'm looking at his facial expressions, at the mockery in his eyes, at sneers on his face as he's listening to the witness's answers, which is really embarrassing for the witness. I've been looking at him constantly, and I think that this should be stopped. The witness should be provided with optimum conditions to be able to his questions. This is a gentleman who is rather quick, but he reacted vehemently while I was examining him so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... and listen carefully the question with your ears and there won't be any problem. Right. Mr. Laws. Mr. Bagaric, look at me. Don't look at Mr. Scott or Mr. Laws -- Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Having expelled Muslims from the west to the east, the HVO saw to it that their supply routes were cut off. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. This was a result of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And then shelled that area and deployed snipers against its people. That's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Let me ask the accused not to -- not to make comments loudly. If he wants to speak, Mr. Praljak would like to speak, let him ask us to let him give the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you will have an opportunity to speak on this, so it's not necessary for the moment to say anything. The Prosecutor is putting his case. You have another one. So it's not necessary to engage in a debate now. In a few days you will be talking to me and all this will be debated. Today there is a doctor who is bearing testimony. There will be some military aspects, certainly. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, Judge Antonetti. I was not going to object and so on and so forth. However, when I examined witnesses, you limited me very carefully, and you asked me precisely what questions should be put to various people. The doctor was supposed to talk about different things, not about sniping fire. Now he's being asked whether people were expelled by somebody. This person hasn't a clue about that. This was never raised in the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... please, and I'm very nearly finished. Can we turn back, please, back to where we started, which is you as a politician and a doctor, all right, Dr. Bagaric. Would you turn please to P06379, the binder in front of you.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: This is an extract from the Official Gazette for the 3rd of November, 1993, and it's decision on the appointment of the commission for investigating war crimes in the territory of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna; all right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can see the document, yes. I can see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Did I understand you to say what that you were not sure that that Ivan Bagaric at number 6 was you, or having thought about it, do you think that is you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did give it a thought, Mr. Prosecutor. It says Ivan Bagaric here, and it is on paper. However, nobody ever gave me that paper. I never participated in any commission of the kind. Nobody ever informed me about this commission, and I am claiming this with full responsibility before the Trial Chamber. If I can be of any assistance, then I can say that this Ivan Bagaric here, as it says, there's a colleague of mine whose name is Ivan Sarac, and the two of us got mixed up very often. We were close. We were both doctors. We were both deputies in the parliament in Sarajevo. He was in charge of the civilian health care. I was in charge of the military health care. We cooperated. So this may be a typo, a mistake. I don't know anything about this. I never saw this document before I came here. I never saw it before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: At number 9 is Mr. Kostroman, who was the gentleman who we saw took the minutes of that meeting in Tomislavgrad that we started with yesterday at 2.15 that you were at, someone you had known a long while by then.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not the case. I did not know Mr. Kostroman either long or well. I would not have signed the minutes then. I would not sign the minutes now because it was a nonsense. Anybody who wrote that, even if it was Kostroman, what he wrote was a sheer nonsense.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: This was a commission set up to investigate crimes against Croats, and it was only interested in crimes against Croats, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object. He's indicated he hasn't seen the document, he doesn't know anything about this commission, he didn't participate in this commission; so now posing questions at this point in time is an absurdity and a waste of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Either you have some elements who contradict what the witness have said, because the witness answered Ms. Nozica saying he didn't know anything about this committee or commission, he never heard about it, and he just discovers this document. So either you have some elements which says that he's lying, which show that he's lying and you can show them to me or you pass to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, apart from his naming being on it together with somebody at number 9 who was a political acquaintance of his for over two years, apart from that I've nothing to show that it's him, but we submit that's a perfectly sufficient foundation for us to say that -- that it might be him and then ask him about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if he's indicated he doesn't know anything about it, what's the purpose of asking? And then not only that, but he's putting the spin as far as what the document pertains, pertains to. So how can he possibly comment? It's an absurdity. In no courtroom -- I don't think that they would allow this in the UK. They certainly wouldn't in the United States, and we both come from a common law system. This is an utter absurdity at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: It's not an absurdity at all. If I had a document with the name Michael Karnavas on it, I could ask Mr. Karnavas some questions about it. I wouldn't have to give up as soon as he says, That's not me. Otherwise -- otherwise prosecutions would be very short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everybody agrees on the fact that you may ask questions because there is the name on this document which shows that legally he was a member of the committee. Now, the question is did he take part in meetings of this committee? He says he didn't. Therefore I'm going to give you another example. A Judge of this Tribunal a few months ago was elected at the ICC, but he hasn't yet been installed there. It's not because there is name on the document that this means that the person question has taken office. So maybe in his case is most probably him on this document, but if he hasn't been in a meeting of this committee or commission what more can he say? Unless you have documents to show it, then show them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... abide by your ruling, Mr. President, but the Judge in question would almost certainly know of his appointment. This is published in the Official Gazette together with names, one of which is somebody that this gentleman knows. All I want to do is explore with him whether it's really him or not. We had this yesterday, that we were in some doubt that he was there in Tomislavgrad.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, Your Honour. I apologise. The question was whether the objective of this commission was to investigate war crimes committed over Croats and then my learned friend intervened. How can anybody know what the objective of commission was if he never worked in that commission? That was the intervention, and since that intervention everything becomes nonsensical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You raised your hand. Did you know anything about this document which was published in the Official Gazette? This is the only question I'm asking now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. The times are hard. I never saw an Official Gazette in Herceg-Bosna. I never looked at any Official Gazettes, and I claim with full responsibility that never handed me this document. If this commission ever existed, then I'm not that person. It must be somebody else. I was never a member of that commission. I never heard of it, and I claim that with full responsibility before you here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to leave the committee, Dr. Bagaric. See if you can help me with this, I want to follow through on with your role of politics: In June of 1994, on the 11th of June, 1994, is it right that you were part of a delegation of Bosnian Croats who went to meet Franjo Tudjman to discuss the Washington Accords?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I was. I apologise what was the date?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just want to draw your attention to the fact that the date is outside of the scope of the indictment. I don't know whether the Trial Chamber can issue a ruling or a decision on that, but I believe that we are beyond the indictment on this -- at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: This witness isn't charged with anything in the indictment and I hope it was clear I'm looking at his political career. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: You were part of that delegation in which the Washington Accords were discussed amongst the Bosnian Croats with President Tudjman; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was a deputy in the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and on one occasion President Tudjman invited all the deputies, everybody who could have a bearing on the further developments with regard to this agreement. I was, indeed, at a meeting. I don't know whether it's the meeting that the Prosecutor is referring to. If you can show me any documents, then I will tell you immediately whether I was there or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Your answer's quite sufficient. The position is this: You had a political clear involved with Herceg-Bosna from 1991 through to 1994, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not true. My political career started in 1990 and ended in 1998 in Bosnia, and I did what I told you about. I discharged certain duties, and I was part of the structures while the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna existed, and I contributed. But let me stop there. This will take us too far. I don't want to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I generally don't think we're disagreeing. You were part of the political apparatus of Herceg-Bosna for the period with which we are concerned. Perhaps before and perhaps after, but for the period with which we're concerned, you're there as part of the politics of Herceg-Bosna and its political apparatus. You agree with that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither yes nor no. I can't say that I was. I did not feel like part of the political apparatus, because I was dealing with the wounded and the sick. That was my duty. In formal terms, I was -- because I remained a deputy. There were no new elections. No new deputies were elected from 1990, so I remained a deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And at the same time as you've said, you were dealing with the injured and the sick, and with people who died, no doubt, in your care.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, not with people who died, no. People who died, no. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Patients --

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not the job of --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: We can't agree about anything, Dr. Bagaric, but let's agree with this then: You were dealing with the injured and the sick. Is that enough for you if I leave out the word "died"? You were dealing with the injured and the sick.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indirectly, yes. I did not treat people. I just organise and supported the system that implemented health care. I personally did not treat people, although I am a physician. There was no time for me to treat anybody. I didn't have the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: The system that was allowing you to treat them was the same system that was adding to their number, wasn't it, in the camps and in East Mostar and at Sovici, the three areas that you have testified about. That's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And you, sir, knew that to be the position and you went along with it. That's also the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I knew that the situation was difficult, that it was war and that my people and Bosnia-Herzegovina was under threat; and as a deputy in the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I participated and I agreed to participate in the defence of the state and the people; and I did that all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And the state that you were assisting was, to your knowledge, committing crimes against people, wasn't it? You knew that it was in the camps, you knew that it was in East Mostar, and you continued to play your part politically nonetheless, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. Your Honours, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel, you intervene precisely in the moment when the witness should answer a question which the Prosecution was -- had a right to ask. I don't understand why you are on your feet. Let the witness answer. It's in your interest. You immediately ask for the floor, and you read the transcript. We will have the impression that you influence the answer. Let the witness answer. That's what I don't understand. Why do you -- are you on your feet, or there is a mistake somewhere?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I thought you would intervene. I was mistaken then. My learned friend just said that this witness was not an accused. If this kind of question may be put to the witness, then I obviously am mistaken. I don't know what I'm doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First, the Prosecutor didn't say he had committed crimes. He told him, "To your knowledge, crimes were committed." He didn't say that he took part or participated, unless the Prosecution -- can you ask your question again, Mr. Laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: It's asked. It's never going to be answered because it's a question which is one that doesn't appeal to those opposite, and so there's not going to be an answer. The witness has now been told precisely what to say and what not to say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to answer. Why not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The witness is going to answer it. He is going to answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness will answer. Mrs. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. I really kindly ask you to look at the way the question was worded. If the witness was asked whether he was on the side that started and continued, and your country was that -- if what I said was not correct, then you are allowed to reprimand me, but I totally believe that the witness has been put in the position of an accused with this question. The witness has not listened to anybody so far. He can say what he wants, but I'm duty-bound to say what I've just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an intervention, just one word in my learned friend Laws's question. It's in line 23 and starts with the following words in English: [In English] "And the state that you were assisting was ..." [Interpretation] I object to the word "state," because this word implies that this witness will confirm that Herceg-Bosna was considered a state. This will then be used as proof that it was a state within a state and can this be clarified, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had the same objection as my learned friend Alaburic. However, even before that, look at the line before that. The Prosecutor asks on page 35, 23, "and the state --" immediately before that in lines from 18 through 22 this witness explained that this was a war and that his people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and he's talking about his duty and mandate as a deputy in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So the witness is talking about Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the Prosecutor is trying to turn the tables on the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That if we had a halfwit in front of us, yes, then you should intervene; but we have here somebody who studied, who is a member of parliament, who has got responsibilities, who understands the questions and was going to answer it. So answer, please, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Your Honours. I said this because of the witness, because the witness has been entrapped. I don't have any doubt that everybody else has understood and that everybody else knows what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, when we are talking about duty of a deputy, and when I'm talking about being a deputy, I'm talking about being a deputy in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was a republic at the time, which is now no longer a republic. After the Dayton Accords, it's only Bosnia-Herzegovina. And when I said my people then I meant the entire Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and whoever was living there. When I assisted and organise things, this was done at a time, Mr. President, when there was a fully blown aggression by the Serbs, and Bosniaks and Croats organise the resistance together. Later on the two victims, unfortunately, conflicted, which ended in a very detrimental outcome, and I never contributed to any of that. On the contrary. I tried as best as I could to reduce the suffering. We organise the health care service which assisted and helped everybody irrespective of their ethnic affiliation and which involved people of all ethnic backgrounds. And when it comes to the detention centres, camps, or whatever you want to call them, I claim before this Trial Chamber with all responsibility that doctors, not me specifically, but there were doctors who were in charge of those detention centres; but when we saw that nothing was in place for such events and for such developments, then we called people who knew what to do. Then we set up teams within the centres. We supported the teams from the outside. And before this Trial Chamber, I claim with full responsibility that we helped prevent a large-scale suffering of the people in the camps at the time when hatred was -- when camps were rife with hatred, and thank God we have prevented epidemics that might have taken higher toll. And with the help and the support of all the others, I claim with full responsibility that the health care takes credit for that. And if God forbid things would have continued, I would still have been helping. I would still be assisting. I really don't understand what is my mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just an intervention with respect to the record. As far as I was able to see, the interpreters translated all this in excellent fashion, everything that Dr. Bagaric said, but on page 39, line 9, when he spoke about these events it says and for such developments the witness used the word unexpected, "neocekivani," unexpected developments; and I think that that word unexpected is very important for the Trial Chamber to be able to weigh up the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have answered the question of the Prosecutor. We agree, don't we?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I have no more questions. Thank you, Dr. Bagaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Laws. We are now going to break for 20 minutes, and we will see for redirect after 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bagaric, I'm going to deal with several topics, the first of which is that proposal of yours, the one you spoke about, that the hospital on the east bank, with the help of the international community, be converted to a joint hospital -- yes, the west bank. I misspoke. Anyway, a hospital which would treat all patients, all people sick both from the east and from the west bank. Now, could you tell the Trial Chamber once again where the hospital was located on the west bank, how far it was from the front line, and so on?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The hospital, which I meant and which you're talking about now, was located several hundred metres or even less, a couple of hundred metres, from the front line, quite literally; and it had other facilities, too, which could have been used had the proposal been put into effect. So the hospital worked throughout that unfortunate conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: That was supposed to be my second question. You say it worked and was operational throughout the conflict; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, did it treat everyone, all citizens and soldiers regardless of ethnicity? Did everybody have access to health care and protection during the war, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never ever during the war did I hear about anybody being withheld medical treatment on ethnic grounds or religious grounds. The hospital treated everybody across the board. And had it been otherwise, I would have heard about it. I would have known about it, and that's why I can say that I don't think anything like that ever happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, you said that it was shelled all the time. I'm just taking you slowly through what you've already said. We have enough topics to discuss, and I'd like to give you an opportunity to answer if you didn't have the time to do so before this. So what was its situation like at the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As it was in the encirclement it was in, the kind of environment that it was in, I can't say that it was shelled with one or another type of weapon, but it was considerably damaged, and that went on throughout the conflict. And at the end of the war, it was in a very sorry state. I know that instead of the windows and the glass, they put plastic sheeting and so on. So, yes, it had its scars.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, Judge Antonetti asked you about your observation to the effect that if the hospital, according to your proposal which you made on several occasions, were to be transferred into a hospital to treat both the sick on the east and the west bank, and if security was provided for it by the international forces and controlled by the international organisations, then it could have influenced, let me say this in the mildest terms, it could have influenced the course of the war. Now, because of Judge Antonetti's question, and he said that this was the first time that anybody of ever mentioned this in the courtroom, to explain why you considered that it could have influenced the course of the war. Why did you say that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had that happened, well, that would have been a sign to everyone, to the Croats and Muslim Bosniaks, showing them that serious attempts were being made to stop the war. That's the first point. And secondly, with the hospital functioning and in such a sensitive place, then it would have been necessary to stop the fighting in that area; and that in turn would mean that the military activities would have been vastly reduced, the activities going on in that district. So had this been accepted, had the proposal been accepted, this could have been a point, an area from which trust would have grown, the seeds of trust would have grown and spread and had a positive influence both on Central Bosnia, because Central Bosnia, let me just repeat this, just as Nova Bila, the hospital in Nova Bila was in poor position in just the same bad position as East Mostar was, and perhaps even worse because they were put up in a church, which was quite inadequate. The facility was quite inadequate, and they didn't have the type of support from the international community. They received aid, too, but I think that this side, that is to say the east bank, was under greater supervision and was more in the focus of attention.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, we heard during the cross-examination conducted by my learned friend that the assistance you offered to the hospital in East Mostar -- well, we heard about that, and that this was due to political pressure. Now, we saw without a doubt throughout the documents that you did provide that assistance and aid. Just let me finish, please. We looked through the documents, and my first question to you is this: Was this kind of aid and assistance -- was more aid and assistance given than we were able to show from the documents we presented?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am quite convinced that there was more aid and assistance. However, all the aid, whatever it was, or -- was significant, but also symbolic. It wasn't enough to solve the problem of the east bank, far from it, but it was an important gesture, and its importance went beyond the quantities, and it had nothing to do with international pressure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, a follow-up question. Quoting from my memory, I don't have the exact documents or references, but it seems to me that in the East Mostar hospital there were Croats who were treated, and also some Croats had been made prisoners. They had been treated by the East Mostar doctors. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do believe that that was the case, especially people who were incarcerated, who ended up in hospital, were certainly treated. And I remember on one occasion the UNHCR, when we asked to see what had happened to one of the prisoners, one of our prisoners, because the International Red Cross said he was in hospital, they said that they didn't have enough blood for a blood transfusion for him; and I remember that we sent a large quantity of blood so that he could be given a blood transfusion. I know that they had problems on that score, so that's how I know that they did take in our people. When I say "our people," I mean of our ethnicity, Croatian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second follow-up question also quoting from memory, but I happen to have a good memory. There was a doctor in this East Mostar hospital who lived in West Mostar; and he had an ID card which enabled him or allowed him to cross, so to say, the front line. So he'd leave West Mostar, went to work to the hospital, came back to West Mostar, et cetera. Were you aware of that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, I must say I didn't know about that. Now, if that happened, it happened from time to time. There was certainly periods when it was very difficult to implement this, but I do know that there were doctors who, for example, were on the west bank but continued working on the east bank. And I know that one of my colleagues, when I worked in Sarajevo after the war in the Ministry of Health he was working in the ministry together with me after the war he said that a surgical team would go from Sarajevo to help the hospital out. So there was a certain amount of communication both ways but limited.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, we were discussing the aid and assistance which you said was very real, but you also say that it was symbolic. Can you explain to the Court about the Nova Bila hospital? It was under siege by which army?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The BH Army. The siege was manned by the BH Army throughout.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And what larger hospitals of the BH Army -- or, rather, of Bosnia-Herzegovina were close to this hospital in Nova Bila?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's a very important question. The hospital in Nova Bila, Your Honours, well, Nova Bila is part of Travnik municipality. Let me say that first, and Travnik had a big important hospital during Yugoslavia, the times of Yugoslavia, and it was a very modern hospital, and the distance between the two was perhaps some 20 kilometres. I can't be quite sure. Perhaps less.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But the town of Zenica is close by. Did it have a hospital? How big was the hospital, and was that hospital under BH Army control as well?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zenica is a large town, and it had a hospital, and it was about half an hour's drive away. It was a very large general hospital with many doctors and a large medical staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, the doctors from these two hospitals, did they provide blood, medicines? Did they take in patients from the Nova Bila hospital as you did, taking in patients from the hospital in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say either yes or no here. I don't know that anything like that ever happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do I understand you to say that you never knew of them providing any help along those lines? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I meant. And I mean the hospital in Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. That was my question. Now, to the best of your recollections, what about the other enclaves? What was the situation like there, Turija, Zabrdje, Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zepce.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, Zepce.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, each of those enclaves in it's own way had its own story to tell and its own unfortunate circumstances.
