And when speaking about health care there, I know for sure that it was at a primitive level because they didn't have sufficient quantities of doctors let alone specialists.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to carry on dealing with these issues, and I'd like to apologise to the Trial Chamber because I'm going to bring up some documents that we've already seen. I prepared some of them yesterday, because I knew I was going to need them. Anyway, my learned friend started out from putting to you that the aid you gave, you gave as the result of political pressure exerted upon Croatia, and he expressed this in quite precise terms. He said that this happened from June onwards. So he said the summer, the summer onwards. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's important for me to say the following: Of course Croatia in a way endeavoured to bring the conflict to an end. That was in the Croatian interest. However, I say with full responsibility here before this Trial Chamber and in public and before my colleague and in the eyes of God that that has nothing to do with any pressure, pressure per se as such, the support that we wanted to give and did give and always tried to provide.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, what you've just said now, let's take a look at that through documents and look at the documents that I'm going to put up on e-court. We looked through them together. First of all, 2D318 [Realtime transcript read in error, "2D138"] and it's --

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you -- you never showed me that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Maybe I didn't, but just listen to me. It is the public statement signed by you, Ivan Bagaric, and Dr. Nusret Dzeko, and it is dated the 23rd of April, 1993. It's the public announcement. And there was no political pressure, and we see from this document that you tried to resolve these problems jointly. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. That is continuation of the story dating back to the end of 1992 when I tried to establish contact with the opposite side, and the only person who was accessible at that time was in Dzeko, the chief of the Medical Corps of the 4th Corps, and I asked that we hold a meeting and state that we health workers did not wish to take part in the war. We do not support the war, and we asked that the victims of the aggression, Muslims and Croats, should be -- do everything in their power to prevent a conflict, and if a conflict did break out that the doctors and entire medical staff should try and work together and help everyone regardless of ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, take a look at document 2D319, please. And before we see it on e-court, I would like to remind you that it is your order appointing a surgical team for Jablanica and after the conflict with the BH Army there in that area; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The document will come up on our screens in just a moment.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know what that's about.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And this is May, too, 1993, far before the period --

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the conflict in Mostar but after the conflict -- well, not conflict -- well, yes, let's call it a conflict. After the suffering of the Croats in Konjic, Trusina, Kostajnica, Sajonica [phoen], Busce [phoen], Trusina, and the other places there. So after that, because you could -- you could still go up there. You could still go to Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: As we can see this happened in the month of May 1993. That is before the summer of 1993.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And now I would like to make a correction. On page 47, line 8, the document number should be 2D318 rather than 138 as it has been recorded, although we have seen the correct document in e-court. And now let's look at P2291. And let me remind you that the date is 11 May 1993, and this is an approval to send blood with the help of the Spanish Battalion, and you commented about this and said that this was part of the assistance sent to the hospital in East Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. However, from distance, I can't be sure whether this is exactly what we have just discussed recently. In any case, I can't tell you exactly what this is but this is it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We are going to have another document regarding the dispatch of blood?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that case this is not it. This is something else.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now you're confusing me. This is a dispatch of blood for the hospital in East Mostar. Is that it? You confirmed that on examination-in-chief, did you not? In the first sentence.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, look at 2D455. My learned friend showed you what Mr. Tudjman said at a meeting, the meeting that was held on the 15th of September, and he said at that political pressure was exerted and that you did what you did under political pressure.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What 15 September?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. This could have only been in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, please trust me just for a moment. Let's not call up the document again. The date is -- or the year is 1993. However, look at your own request. This is your request on the 16 of September, one day later, and in this request the last sentence is very important. You say here: "We kindly ask you to help the Muslim side for the treatment of civilians, especially women and children, in the war hospital in Mostar and in the other HVO hospitals." So this is not the idea of a joint hospital. You're offering treatment in the hospital in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, if this was done because of a political pressure, how can that be tied to the last sentence where it says: "We are doing this for only one reason, which is humanitarian reason. Therefore, we kindly ask you not to make any political connotations to this." But if you had done things under political pressure, wouldn't it have been logical to exploit this offer of yours in political -- in political --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: But it does sound like a somewhat leading question, with respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please try to be neutral. Thank you, Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Prosecutor please turn off the microphone. The objection was correct. Let me rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did your final message have a political background or a political connotation?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It has nothing whatsoever to do with any political pressures. I'm not -- it is not my intention to waste your time. However, all this time I'm trying this think what kind after meeting took place in Zagreb. I believe that I never attended any meetings in Zagreb in 1993. I attended meetings in Zagreb in 1994 after the signing of the Washington Peace Accords.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, ignore the meeting. Ignore the meeting. The Prosecutor showed you a document about the meeting that Mr. Boban attended together with Mr. Tudjman on the 15th of September, 1993. This is P5080, if you will. It was shown to you during cross-examination. Just a moment, please. You asked me what the document was. I'm trying to clarify. And in that document you see that Dr. Tudjman said that there was a major political pressure put to bear on Croatia, and with this regard my learned friend questioned you and asked you whether you, yourself, because of the political pressure, as of the summer 1993 onwards, assisted and offered assistance as may be seen from the document. So this is the link. Does that make you any more clear?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, yes, I was confused. I thought that -- that the gentleman was talking about a meeting in which I participated. I never knew about this meeting between Boban and Tudjman, and I never received any instruction from anybody, and no link could be established between the two.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And just two more documents about you further activities. The first one is 2D333. This is your order to send an ambulance to Mrs. Sally Baker to help her transport the wounded from the left to the right bank of the Neretva. I want to present this as another type of activity which took place on the 15th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: On the day when the meeting took place it would not be possible for you technically to be aware of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This has nothing whatever to do with the meeting, Mrs. Sally Baker, and we prepared this much earlier. The preparations had lasted for days.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And now look at 2D00328, another document that we have already seen. This document confirms that the war hospital -- or, rather, its transfusion service issues a certain quantity of blood.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, and finally although you have already spoken about this, but let's bring the matter home. When it comes to extending your hand or extending assistance to the wounded on the other side, were your colleagues governed by any political reasons?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. Nobody ever exerted any pressure on me, and I never did those things as a politician. I did them as a physician who was involved in that war, and before the war was -- happened to be a politician.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And now let's move on to the topic of detention centres and questions with this regard. Could you please look in my pink binder. I have put together some very important documents about some of the things that you mentioned. They are in a chronological sequence. Could you please look at 2D754, which is a report.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It arises from this report, Mr. Bagaric, that an on-site inspection was carried out in -- at the Heliodrom pursuant to a telephone conversation with Stanko Bozic, the head of the SV. Mr. Bagaric, can you confirm that this was how your service for infectology and epidemiology, whenever they received a call or an invitation they would go and do what was necessary?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were already doctors there. There were already physicians, local physicians there. However, when an intervention was needed at a higher specialist level, we had that service. Then we intervened, and this is a just an example of how this was done.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm asking you this, Mr. Bagaric, because of the document that the Prosecutor showed you, and you said that you don't know whether you received it or not from Mr. Stanko Bozic. We will come to that document as well. However, in e-court you will see another document which was subsequently introduced, and this is P4145. You will see it in e-court. P4145. Very well. We have the correct document. This is your first request. I've already showed you that document. A lot was said about the transport of the wounded and sick from the Heliodrom and how that should have been done. I'm drawing your attention to the last line in which you said: "Until we have the -- an ambulance for the Heliodrom, please use the vehicles of the operation zone South-East Herzegovina and the war hospital in Mostar." Was it how things were done?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was done, and my departure to Canada was linked with the purchase of ambulances that we did not have. The Croatian Community over there offered to help us. This did not happen before the end of the year. We always lacked vehicles. We had a shortage of vehicles all the time. We could not deal with the problem, and this is actually a proposal submitted by the unit there how to resolve the problem or how to deal with the problem temporarily.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Just for further clarification, can we say that this was on 12 August 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you please look at the second document in my pink binder, which is 2D412. Mr. Bagaric, this is your order dated the 28 September 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This will appear very often in subsequent document. My learned friend Pinter asked you whether this document was ever forwarded to the Main Staff. You said no, and it's obvious from the document itself; am I right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And now in temporal sequence --

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I be allowed to say something very briefly?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Go on.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the English translation here I have noticed that already. After -- there is a question mark, and here it should say 18 August. Our order, therefore, was issued on the 18th of August. There is a question mark here showing that the -- the date was illegible, and I believe that this should be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, please look at the Croatian. The date is illegible?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I know what it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, if you say so, we will make a correction in the document, and we're grateful for your intervention. It was indeed on the 18th of August. Very well. Could you please look at P5465. This is a letter of which you said that you don't know whether you received it. Mr. Bagaric, your order were issued a day -- one day before. The previous order was issued one day before.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It was the day before?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one day before.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This regulates the transport of sick, which was regulated pursuant to your request dated 12 August; is that correct? This is document P4145.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, as to whether this document was ever sent to you or not, let's look at the following document, which is P5503.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Just one day after the letter sent by Mr. Bozic, which we don't know whether you received it or not. It says that there was a three-member commission, including Mr. Stanko Bozic, and that there was an inspection.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Does it say anywhere in this document that Mr. Bozic points to anything that refers to the document that he allegedly sent and which you may have received or not? Is there anything that would point to that document?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just bear with me for a moment, please. Only the part in which it says: "Seriously wounded and sick should be transported to the regional hospital." I believe that this is the only reference. And the rest was all the result, i.e., there was no reference to any existing problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, I asked you at the beginning whether this type of transport of sick and wounded was also regulated pursuant to your order issued in August.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, and as far as I can remember as I sit here today, this was being dealt with between the hospital and the operation zone, and I intervened only if something was not functioning properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: As my learned friend showed you yesterday, this document was sent to several addresses, to the Main Staff included, and my learned friend asked you about your order and whether it was submitted to the Main Staff. I would like to ask you whether an attachment to this document is your order dated 28 September 1993.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And now let's look at the first page, and I'll tell you why. We saw several documents which were addressed to Mr. Bruno Stojic, and we will come to them. First of all, on the original of this document my learned friend [indiscernible] intervened regarding the stamp that was erroneously corrected in English. This is not it. This was properly corrected. Can you look at the receipt stamp. Is this the receipt stamp of the Croatian Defence Council of the Defence Department in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So there is a receipt stamp showing that it was received in the Defence Department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have spoken about these documents which the situation, and this was insisted by the Prosecutor, and now I'm going to draw attention once again to a document that you have before you which is P5035. This is a report by the Spanish delegation --

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Can you repeat the number of the document?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: P5035 should be the next in your binder. I'll draw your attention to item number 7, which is a visit to the detention camp at the Heliodrom. The documents that we have seen so far were produced in late September 1993, and this one was -- is dated 14 September 1993. Let me just draw your attention to item 7 and the part of this document where it says there are two outpatient clinics. This is the penultimate passage on page 6: "There are two outpatient clinics with one physician each and several medical staff. There are no health problems."

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see that. I apologise. What is the page in Croatian?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It is page 6 in Croatia. Item 7 penultimate page on --

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: There are two infirmaries with one doctor, no health problems; is that right? Is that what was noted here?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bagaric, did you know that the military structures -- that someone from the military structures sent teams of doctors to solve problems to -- in the central military prison and the Gabela and Dretelj centres?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you know that some other teams of doctors, apart from the ones that you contacted with, were examined, the detainees and prisoners in Gabela, Dretelj, and Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The doctors who were there worked there. The doctors who were incarcerated there, as well as doctors from outside, from the brigades which covered the whole territory and also the military district and doctors -- or, rather, not doctors but Dr. Ivan Curic, first and foremost, who was a specialist and the head of department, as support to all this.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you take a look at the next document, P3197, please.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is an order by Mr. Nedjeljko Obradovic dated the 3rd of July, 1993, and here it is what it says: "In order to ensure health care for the prisoners that doctors' commission should be set up for the medical care and examination and treatment of prisoners for the prisons in Gabela, Dretelj, and Heliodrom, Mostar, and pursuant to the following order: "After examining the prisoners, those who are the most needy, those who are the sickest or those who should be released or be sent for treatment to note them down and send in a written request to me and the chief of the Medical Corps of the 1st and 3rd HVO brigades will be responsible for the excuse of this order to me." So are those the persons, the doctors that you said also provided medical care? But we have the mention of a medical commission here.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That does refer to those doctors, although I have to acknowledge that I've never seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, this is an exhibit. This document is already an exhibit. I'm not asking you to confirm the authenticity of the document, just to say whether it is the same team of doctors.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The transcript had stopped for a moment, and I'm trying to follow. Now, Dr. Bagaric, I'm going to show you two documents that you saw yesterday during the cross-examination with short questions. The first one is P4312. It should be the second document. 4352 is the document number, 4352.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I don't think that that's the right document. Ah, it will come up. Now, I'm going to ask you some brief questions about that document. Has it got a stamp showing that it was received?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You said yesterday that if Bruno Stojic had received this document, and I'm going to ask you now, did you ever talk to Bruno Stojic, and did he ever tell you anything which would relate to this document?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And let me ask you directly, do you know if Bruno Stojic ever received this document?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot know that. There's no way that I can know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Now, the next document is P5812. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I have to repeat the question. Has it got a registration stamp or stamp saying that it was received?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you ever talk about anything which would allow you to conclude that Mr. Stojic had received this document?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that information. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: At the insistence of my client to make everything quite clear and to make certain once again, let's look at the document that you have once again, or you can look at it on your screen. It is P5503. So that we can have a look once again what that stamp of the Defence Department looks like, the registration stamp. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's go back to document P5812 now. You spoke about this document yesterday. You said you knew nothing about it, but you did offer a comment -- or, rather, you commented on some of the details contained in this document, and, Mr. Bagaric, you also said that it was only at the collegium of the Defence Department, on the 2nd of September, that you heard of the distance between military prisons, right, and the place -- or, rather, the centres where the prisoners of war were being held, right? Or, rather, that you couldn't differentiate between the two; right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to draw your attention to the following. Although we see that there was no incoming stamp that proving that Mr. Stojic received this, however, look at point 3 and what the document says there, what Mr. Bozic says, point 3. The unresolved status of the central military prison and an appointment should be made for the person who will be in charge of the prison, and then it says: "The prison cannot be organised on the basis of two organisational wholes but must function as one entity, one whole." Now, Mr. Bagaric, did you know that this SVZ or central military prison was a military prison for members of the HVO who had committed crimes? So a classical type of military prison. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't be quite precise. I don't know. I really can't give you a right -- a proper answer. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. I won't insist upon that then. Now, Judge Antonetti asked you something yesterday which I considered to be very important, and it was about the -- well, you were shown a document about the fact that doctors had been detained after 1993, and Judge Antonetti asked you how you experienced this. I'm going to ask you about your direct knowledge about the conduct and behaviour of doctors, the doctors who were on this side or the Bosniak doctors who were on this side and crossed over to that side, because we were discussing whether a doctor can be detained, or whatever, or merit being detained, heaven forbid, but were there situations of that kind?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just be able to say one sentence and then I'll answer your question? With the Court's indulgence may I have the Court's permission to make a comment. I think the witness who testified more than one, two, or three days that it would be very useful for one and all if there were to be an institute for correcting erroneous quotations, which means -- or statements. When I sleep on something, then perhaps I would rethink something that I had already said, and I think that I should be given the right to put myself right, to correct what I had already said. And yesterday when I said that most of these people here I assume were not guilty of anything because that was what the Prosecutor wanted to hear. He asked, "Are they guilt?" So I want to correct myself, because I haven't seen the names. I hadn't seen the that child you saw. So the correction I would like to make when I said that nobody is guilty until something is proved, particularly not with respect to women and children. That is understood. Now, so far as this question is concerned -- now, to answer your question, I can't speak about names now, and I don't wish to speak about names. They were my colleagues, doctors. However, I do know for certain that a lot of complaints were made with respect to one doctor that was in charge of a whole area over there and under whose command our people alleged that a lot of -- well, lots of things happen, crimes and so on. Now, I heard about this. I can't say whether that is the truth of the matter or not, but I also heard that one of our colleagues, our doctors who was in the HVO, during that night or day when there was the turnaround, where weapons were turned on their colleagues, he took his colleague, a doctor, a Croat, he took him into custody. He arrested him. Now, this colleague of ours who was arrested survived. Nothing happened to him, but he was incarcerated. He was held in detention, and that's something I heard at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bagaric, I'm not going to insist upon this, but when you spoke that first doctor, just tell us what area he worked in.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bijelo Polje, that general area, around Mostar. Oh, you mean the first doctor. Well, Konjic and that general area, from Sarajevo towards Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So the first from the Konjic area and the second example was Bijelo Polje; right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's just look at one more document.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to apologise and say that I have no personal evidence and proof of that. I just know that those were the rumours going round.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, I do respect that, Witness. I understand that, and I -- there's no need for you to speak about proof and evidence, but here's a document that can. 2D857 is the number, and it is the last document in my binder. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And it is a request for launching an investigation against -- well, it's the 22nd of July. That's the date of it. You have an indictment there, and the first name is Samir Kreso. Now, let's look at page 3 of that document. Let's turn to page 3. And let me remind you that on the first page it says doctor who was a member of the 2nd Brigade of the 1st Battalion. HVO 2nd Brigade, 1st Battalion, member of. Now, in this indictment mention is made of the fact that this particular gentleman, on the 30th of June, 1993, from Zlatic, Dragan's house tricked Rajic, Filip, and took him away; and after arresting him, wounded him, took him in an unknown direction, then set a house on fire. Well, you can all read that. Anyway, tell us, Mr. Bagaric, I don't want to ask you whether you know this man and the event, but from this it follows that he was a doctor who was a member of the HVO and after that, on the 30th of June crossed over to the Muslim side and joined the Muslim army and then committed what he committed here.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says here, but I really don't know anything about this, whether that was the case or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now I'm going to conclude my examination with some political questions as my colleague did, as my learned friend did, because I haven't addressed that matter yet. Could you explain -- well, we heard here in court many times when the document from the meeting was shown and the conclusions that you said weren't made which insisted that Mr. Izetbegovic said, "This is not our war." Now, since you were an eye-witness to these events, you were in Sarajevo at that time, you were in that general area, how was this understood among the Croatian people, the Croatian population, and why was there such a strong reaction from the Croatian people, and in what context and when was this statement made?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Izetbegovic uttered those words as the president of the Presidency or member of the Presidency or whatever, the man who represented Bosnia-Herzegovina, and as such he represented the Croats as well, the Croat -- the Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina. And he made the statement during the aggression against the Republic of Croatia, and this was, in fact, a terrible insult but also a message to the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina; and it had a terrible ring, because I think it happened, although I can't actually claim that, it came after the attack on the village of Ravno, which, Your Honour, Mr. President, it is a village in the Dubrovnik hinterland with a Croatian majority. It is in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in the true sense of the word genocide was committed there, because all the inhabitants of one of the hamlets, and there were a number of those, were killed. I think seven elderly men or women. They were killed. And that really happened. And I heard certain interpretations that were different implying other things with respect to his statement. But regardless of all that and if we leave that aside, it was a terrible thing to hear. It was a terrible thing for the Croats to hear generally, and particularly in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, my learned friend of the Prosecution said that you from 1991, and you put him right and said that it was from 1990, that you held some political functions, and I'm going to ask you very precisely. Were you in 1990 first a deputy in the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Let's take things in order.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a young physician, due to force of circumstance, with war looming, at the first free elections I was indeed elected a deputy or member of parliament in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And that could be considered to be a political post; right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was a political post.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What did you say? As of roughly March 1991 you joined the main Medical Corps; is that right? 1992?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And then you became the chief and then the assistant to the minister, and you worked as a doctor; right? Just let me finish. You worked as a doctor. So during that time you weren't a politician. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my mandate had not expired, although I didn't deal in politician. I dealt in health care and protection, and I worked in the medical centre as a doctor, and from my elections in 1990, I worked in the health centre in Tomislavgrad. So I did practical work as a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, will you let me finish, please. I want to look at your functions after the signing of the Washington Accords. You were elected assistant minister for health of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. After I completed my specialist training, I worked as assistant minister for the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the field of health protection.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You worked in Sarajevo, did you, at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And did you meet your colleagues who were in the BH Army? I have to ask you that.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very often.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly slow down and not overlap. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're going too fast, and interpreters have problems. Please slow down and wait before you answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Mr. Bagaric finds it hard to wait for me to end my questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, could you please wait and then answer my question. How were you received as a doctor who spent the wartime in the HVO? How were you received by politics in Sarajevo, who at the time were in the BH army? Did you have any problems or were you respected? Were you held in high esteem, and are you still treated the same way?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had studied in Sarajevo, and I had met a lot of my colleagues while studying, and when I returned after the war, I met many of them in Sarajevo; and I have to say with a lot of satisfaction that it never happened that any of them and although we were on two different sides in one part of Bosnia-Herzegovina that in any -- any of -- that none of them had any objections to my work. They all told me that they had heard of my attempts to do good. That's how things were, and I had contacts. I still have contacts, and I believe that this is a nice story with some of the doctors who had left Bosnia and Herzegovina. They are Bosnian Muslims. They live abroad. One of them lives in America, who never fails to send me a Christmas or an Easter card. He was here recently. And many other such people, and I am thankful to God that I have that image and many of them enjoy my respect because they acted as doctors in very dire times.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's why we called you as a witness. Mr. Bagaric, this brings my additional examination to an end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... colleagues. I wish to thank you. You have come at the request of Mr. Stojic to bring your help to find the truth, and you have my best wishes for your return in your country; and I will ask the usher to accompany you until -- to accompany you to the door of the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I apologise for having spoken more and faster than I should have, and thank you for bearing me -- with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we break, I would like to speak to Mr. Vasic [as interpreted] and Mr. Praljak. I looked at the 24 finders which you produced with the list for Mr. Praljak's testimony, and I have noticed that many documents were not translated. Is it when Mr. Praljak will use these documents will we have the translations, Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the documents that will be used Mr. Praljak's testimony will be translated or should be according to plan. Our team adds translations into e-court on a daily basis. If they are not there already, it doesn't mean that they won't be there within five or six days. And as you well know, Dr. -- Mr. Praljak's testimony's going to take a while. In any case, we not going to be using documents, which are not translated unless we're faced with something critical. In that case, we are going to present the original of such a document, and we will take it from there. We are aware of our obligation. You know that our sources are limited, that our access to the translation service is limited, but we are doing our best to translate as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, Mr. Kovacic, since I've been preparing for the hearing for Mr. Praljak for quite a long time, I have noticed the following problem: When he testified in the Naletilic case, and when he answered the cross-examination questions led by Mr. Scott himself, he said that when two documents were submitted to him, that these documents were forged. So personally, I would like to have, and perhaps my colleagues would also like to have, a list of those documents which you deem yourself as being forged.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. My mistake. We did not make any particular plan -- plans to prepare such a list. I know what you're talking about. However, a list can be produced, because we're dealing with only a few documents that we believe are forgery. I'm sure that you will remember that we filed a submission about the document, which we are going to deal with. As far as I can remember, the moment there are a couple of such documents. We will put them on a separate list. Mr. Praljak, I believe, will know better what this is about. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. Whenever somebody says "a couple" or "a few," I find this very difficult to grasp. A couple is two, and documents may be one, two, or three. As far as I remember, and I have believe I do, Mr. Scott showed me just one document in passing, as it were, and for which I claim, and I remember my words, I said that this is not my style, this is not my manner, this is not my handwriting, and this is not my signature. And although this was done in a haste, I still remember that there was a signature, and the person who forged the document tried to imitate my signature. The letter R in my family name Praljak is somewhat curved and not curved in the way I write it, and I have that on hundreds of documents. So this is a very obvious forgery. And there's another document that I remember is a document that somebody else falsified to show that on the 8th of November, 1993, in the evening, added something at the end of Mr. Mijo Jelic's request and approved that detainees should be taken to work. As a general and Main Staff commander, I would never added anything on Mr. Jelic's document. I never approved that anybody be taken to any kind of work let alone to the front line; and also I'm going to demonstrate where I was on the 8th and on 9th in the afternoon and in the evening before I left that area around 7.00, half past 7.00 on the 9th after having handed over duty to General Roso. As I know, there are two documents. Let's be clear on that. Let's make sure that there are not two documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic. Mr. Kovacic, if, and I say if, in the hypothesis that those documents had been forged, how is it possible that those documents were found in the Zagreb archive, official archive were precisely there in official archives? Did you make an inquiry? Did you try and understand how those documents ended up there and that they were submitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, obviously we are going to provide very detailed argument in our final brief, and during our Defence case we're going to provide all the necessary facts that will allow us to tackle the issue in the final brief. However, in brief outlines I can give you the gist of the whole thing. As you may well know, and the Prosecutor certainly does, the documents issued by the HVO HZ HB and HR HB, arrived and nobody has ever confirmed how they arrived. The fact is that these documents did arrive in the Republic of Croatia, and if I tell you the area now, I may be mistaken. However, it was sometime in the late 1990s. At the beginning of the year 2000, the Prosecutor and then the Defence cases that were working on the contemporary cases were given access to those documents. It is not known exactly. There are rumours and speculations, but nothing is -- has been proven for a fact where the vast amounts of documents, and we're talking about several -- tens of thousands of documents, where they had been from the Washington or the Dayton Accords until the moment when they turned up in Zagreb. In this courtroom, the Prosecutor has produced documents showing that in Bosnia and Herzegovina and in Croatia, among the intelligence services and during their competition work there were some conspiracies. I don't intend to try and prove that there were or there weren't. Obviously there were groups and individuals who throughout all that period between 1994 and 2000 expected to be indicted or were afraid that they would be indicted. There were those who harboured their interests to either cover up their traces or to implement somebody or something of the kind. I can't speak of that, and I can't prove anything. However, there's a fact that I -- that I intend to prove. There is a signed and certified statement issued by the then-administrator of the Croatian state archives from which it arises that the documents of whose authenticity you are deciding here are not authentic only because of the fact that they bear the stamp of the state archive. It is only that stamp that will confirm for a fact that the document was located in the Croatian archive in the HZ HB contingent, and that it was copied there. Whether the document is authentic, how it had arrived in the archives, it is something that nobody knows, and we're going to talk about that during our Defence case. There are a few more details. I don't want to bore you with any of them. However, we will bear that in mind. There is one more technical thing. In our pre-trial brief and then during trial on one occasion we proposed an argument that was never responded to, and the argument is as follows: Since both sides to these proceedings are dealing with tens of thousands of documents, you know that only too well because a lot of them end up being admitted into evidence. Both sides only deal with the copies of these documents, and those copies are the first, second, third, or even tenth generation. If any of the sides, either the Prosecutor or us, want to challenge the authenticity and the originality of a certain document, in my position, which is in keeping with many national jurisdictions, then the challenge -- the sides should produce an original. For as long as we all agree that a copy is probably a credible copy and as good as the original, then it's okay. However, this is an accusatory proceedings, and if one side says, No, this is a forgery for this or that reason, that has to be stated, then the other side should be asked to produce the original. In the brief -- in the submission that has just been mentioned and in which we challenge the authenticity of the document that Mr. Praljak has just mentioned in his oral submission, a document where he signed his name under another signature, we demonstrated that it is really a -- very simple and easy to falsify a document of that kind. I repeat, my position is that when a document is challenged the other side has to be asked to produce the original and that applies to both sides equally. If the Prosecutor challenges our document we'll try to prove its authenticity through a witness or maybe we'll be able to produce the original, but that has to be binding on both sides. Obviously you have to decide that at the end of these proceedings, and I would like to thank you for your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Perhaps we leave it at this stage. Perhaps we will have an opportunity to take a look at the documents challenged when your witness or Mr. Praljak testifies. Mr. Praljak, very shortly, what did you want to say? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Judge Antonetti, I would like to ask you -- well, the way in which the documents arrived and were archived and what do we mean by archives, well-ordered archive and so on, that you provide it because I worked to form an archive of the Croatian army after I returned in November; and I know quite a lot about archives and what can be considered archive material and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, for the interpretation, we're talking about two archives. One is the Croatian State Archive, and that is the main source both for the Prosecution and the Defence. The other archive that was mentioned a moment ago, that General Praljak mentioned, and that is also where some documents were found, although to a lesser extent, is the Croatian military archive. That's quite a different institution. It's a different institution altogether. So they should be kept separate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Ms. Nozica, for next week, we have the next witness, two hours for the in chief, an hour for the other Defence teams, and two hours for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. The witness has arrived. This witness had some health problems last time. I haven't seen him yet. He arrived this afternoon, but since he's here I hope everything will be in order and that we stand trial ready for Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. If there are no additional questions, I'll adjourn, and we'll meet Monday at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
